sentences.text: Imagine you are in an interview, and the professor asks you, "What is your favorite theorem?"
Here is mine.
Take the primes five, thirteen, seventeen and twenty-nine.
Each of them is a sum of two squares.
Five is one plus four.
Thirteen is four plus nine.
Seventeen is one plus sixteen.
And twenty-nine is four plus twenty-five.
But three, seven, eleven and nineteen never are, no matter how hard you try.
What separates the two groups?
Divide by four.
The first group leaves remainder one.
The second group leaves remainder three.
This is Fermat's two-square theorem.
Today I want to show you a proof of it that fits in one sentence, and a picture of windmills that explains why that sentence works.
First, the precise statement.
Let p be an odd prime.
Then p can be written as x² + y², with x and y integers, if and only if p is congruent to one, modulo four.
Geometrically, the circle x² + y² = p passes through points of the integer lattice exactly when p is one more than a multiple of four.
The story begins with Fermat.
In a letter to Mersenne, dated Christmas Day, 1640, he stated this theorem and claimed he had a proof.
As usual, he never wrote it down.
That is why it is sometimes called Fermat's Christmas theorem.
The first published proof came more than a century later, from Euler, using a method called infinite descent.
Later came a deeper explanation, through what we now call the Gaussian integers, named after Gauss.
And in 1990, Don Zagier published a paper with a remarkable title.
A one-sentence proof that every prime p congruent to one mod four is a sum of two squares.
It builds on an earlier idea of Roger Heath-Brown.
That one sentence is what we will unpack today.
One direction is easy, and it is worth seeing first.
Every square leaves remainder zero or one when divided by four.
An even number squared is a multiple of four.
An odd number squared is one more than a multiple of four.
Look, the square of an odd number splits into one small square in the middle, plus four equal rectangles.
Keep this little windmill in mind.
We will meet it again.
So a sum of two squares can only be zero, one or two, modulo four.
Never three.
That rules out every prime of the form 4k + 3.
But notice something.
Twenty-one is also one more than a multiple of four, and yet it is not a sum of two squares.
So the condition is necessary, but on its own it is not sufficient.
Primality must matter somewhere in the proof.
Keep this in mind.
We will find exactly where it is used.
The real content of the theorem is the other direction.
Every prime that leaves remainder one really is a sum of two squares.
And that is hard, because it is a pure existence statement.
There is no formula that simply hands you x and y.
So how do you prove that something exists without finding it?
One classic answer is to count.
If you can show that the number of solutions is odd, then it cannot be zero.
And to show that a number is odd, you do not need to count exactly.
You only need to pair things up.
This leads to the key tool, an involution.
An involution is a map from a set to itself that undoes itself.
Apply it twice, and you are back where you started.
An involution splits the set into pairs, a together with f of a, plus some points that are sent to themselves.
Those are the fixed points.
The pairs always contribute an even number.
So the size of the set and the number of fixed points always have the same parity.
Now suppose the same finite set carries two different involutions.
Their numbers of fixed points have the same parity.
In particular, if one of them has exactly one fixed point, the other has an odd number of fixed points, so it has at least one.
If this sounds familiar, it should.
Sperner's lemma is proved with the same kind of parity argument, by counting doors in pairs.
So here is the plan.
We want the solutions we are looking for to appear as the fixed points of an involution.
Since p is odd, one of the two squares must be even.
So we are really looking for p equals x squared plus the square of two y, that is, x² + 4·y·y.
Now comes the creative step.
Replace one of the two y's by a new letter, z.
Consider every triple of positive integers with x² + 4yz = p, and call this set S.
S is finite, because x squared and y z are both smaller than p.
For p equal to thirteen, for example, S has exactly three elements.
This new set has an obvious symmetry.
Swap y and z.
That is an involution, and its fixed points are exactly the triples with y equal to z.
Then p equals x squared plus the square of two y.
Those are precisely the solutions we want.
So the whole theorem reduces to one question.
Is the number of elements of S odd?
And by the parity principle, it is enough to find a second involution on S with exactly one fixed point.
Notice what just happened.
We did not find a symmetry.
We created one, by splitting y times y into y times z.
Making the problem bigger gave us room to move.
To find the second involution, let us draw the equation. x squared is a square of side x.
Four y z is four rectangles, each y by z.
Attach one rectangle to each side of the square, all turning the same way, and you get a windmill whose area is exactly p.
Every element of S is a windmill.
Here are all eleven windmills of area forty-one.
In this picture, swapping y and z simply flips each blade over, so that its length and width trade places.
The fixed windmills are the ones with square blades.
And look.
Four squares of side y fit together into one square of side two y.
So a fixed windmill is literally p, split into two squares.
Now comes the most beautiful observation.
Erase the lines inside a windmill, and keep only its outline.
The outline does not remember how it was cut.
The same outline can often be cut into a windmill in a different way, around a different central square.
Here is the rule.
Look at the four tips of the blades, and draw the square through them.
If that square fits inside the outline, cut along it.
If it does not fit, use the square through the outer edges of the blades instead.
Sometimes the new square is larger, sometimes it is smaller, and sometimes the new windmill turns the other way, like a mirror image.
Written in coordinates, this rule becomes Zagier's famous formula, with three cases.
Cutting again brings back the original windmill, so re-cutting is an involution.
A larger square becomes smaller again, a smaller one becomes larger, and the mirrored case mirrors back.
When is a windmill unchanged by re-cutting?
Exactly when the square through the tips is the central square itself, that is, when x equals y.
And this is where primality enters.
If x equals y, then p equals x squared plus four x z, which is x times (x + 4z).
Since p is prime, x must be one.
So the only fixed windmill is the one with x and y both equal to one, a perfectly symmetric cross.
One more detail.
The rule never gets stuck on a boundary case.
Those cases would need p to be a perfect square, or an even number, and an odd prime is neither.
Now put everything together.
The re-cutting involution has exactly one fixed point, so S has an odd number of elements.
Therefore the flipping involution also has a fixed point, a windmill with square blades.
And that is p, written as a sum of two squares.
This is Zagier's entire proof, and it really is one sentence.
When I first saw the formula, it looked like magic.
But every step has a reason, and the reasons are the most valuable part.
First, we needed existence, not a formula.
Existence follows from an odd count, and an odd count follows from pairing.
Second, to use pairing, the solutions we want must be fixed points.
So we built a set with a built-in symmetry, by splitting y squared into y times z.
Third, we needed a second involution, and the algebra alone gives no hint.
The picture does.
An area that can be cut in two ways is a natural source of pairs.
Fourth, primality is used at exactly one sharp point, to make the fixed point unique.
Test this with twenty-one.
Its set S has two fixed windmills, the cross with x equal to one, and another one with x equal to three.
Two is even, so the argument proves nothing.
And indeed, twenty-one is not a sum of two squares.
This is a good habit in general.
For any proof, ask where exactly each hypothesis is used, and what breaks without it.
There is one more surprise.
The proof seems to say only that a solution exists, but it secretly contains an algorithm.
Start from the cross, the unique fixed point of re-cutting.
Flip the blades.
Re-cut.
Flip again.
Re-cut again.
Every step is forced, and we can never return to a windmill we have already visited.
Since S is finite, the walk must stop, and it can only stop at a windmill that flipping leaves unchanged.
For forty-one, after ten steps we reach blades of size two by two, and we read off that forty-one is five squared plus four squared.
Why does this always work?
Think of each windmill as a dot, and join partners with lines.
Every dot has at most two lines, one of each kind, so the picture breaks into paths and loops.
The cross is the end of a path, and the other end must be a solution.
If you know the proof of Sperner's lemma, this is the same idea as walking through rooms and doors.
It is not the fastest method, though.
For large primes, there are much faster algorithms, based on the Euclidean algorithm.
Now let us zoom out.
Which whole numbers, not just primes, are sums of two squares?
The key is a multiplication rule.
The product of two sums of two squares is again a sum of two squares.
In the language of complex numbers, this just says that the length of a product is the product of the lengths.
Combine this with Fermat's theorem, and you get the full answer.
A positive integer is a sum of two squares exactly when every prime factor of the form 4k + 3 appears an even number of times.
In the Gaussian integers, numbers of the form a plus b i, this becomes a statement about factoring.
A prime that is one mod four splits into two conjugate factors, like five equals (2 + i)(2 − i).
A prime that is three mod four cannot be split.
It stays prime.
Unique factorization in the Gaussian integers also tells us something Zagier's proof does not.
The way of writing p as a sum of two squares is unique, up to order and signs.
And the story continues.
Which primes are x squared plus two y squared?
Two, and the primes that are one or three mod eight.
Which are x squared plus three y squared?
Three, and the primes that are one mod three.
Questions like these lead to quadratic reciprocity, and eventually to class field theory.
And if you allow four squares instead of two, Lagrange proved that every positive integer is a sum of four squares.
What is it good for?
Here are two applications I like.
The first is about right triangles.
If p equals a squared plus b squared, then squaring a plus b i gives a squared minus b squared, plus two a b i.
So a squared minus b squared, two a b, and p form a right triangle with integer sides.
Five gives three, four, five.
Thirteen gives five, twelve, thirteen.
In fact, the odd primes that can be the hypotenuse of an integer right triangle are exactly the primes that are one mod four.
The second is a surprise involving pi.
Count the integer points inside a large circle of radius R.
There are about pi R squared of them.
There is a second way to count the same points, using divisors, and it rests on the theory of sums of two squares.
Comparing the two counts gives Leibniz's formula.
Pi over four equals one, minus one third, plus one fifth, minus one seventh, and so on.
So a question about which primes are sums of two squares ends up connected to geometry, to complex numbers, and even to pi.
That web of connections is a big part of why I love this theorem.
Now let us practice.
Here is how an interview about this theorem might go.
Notice that each answer is short and precise, and leaves something the examiner can follow up on.
So, what is your favorite theorem?
My favorite theorem is Fermat's two-square theorem.
It says that an odd prime is a sum of two squares if and only if it leaves remainder one when divided by four.
I like it because the statement is so simple, but the proof I like best is a clever counting argument that fits in one sentence.
Can you show me why primes of the form four k plus three can't work?
Sure.
Any square is zero or one, mod four.
An even number squared is divisible by four, and an odd number squared is one more than a multiple of four.
So a sum of two squares is zero, one or two, mod four, but never three.
Is that condition enough for any number, not just for primes?
No.
Twenty-one leaves remainder one, but it is not a sum of two squares.
That's because twenty-one is three times seven, and both of those primes are three mod four.
In general, a positive integer is a sum of two squares exactly when every prime factor of the form four k plus three appears an even number of times.
Good.
How would you prove the hard direction?
I'd use Zagier's proof.
Take the set S of positive triples with x squared plus four y z equal to p.
Swapping y and z is an involution, and its fixed points give p as x squared plus the square of two y.
So it's enough to show that S has an odd number of elements.
For that, there's a second involution, which you can picture as re-cutting a windmill, and it has exactly one fixed point.
By parity, S is odd, so the swap has a fixed point too.
Where exactly do you use the fact that p is prime?
Mainly in one place, the uniqueness of the fixed point.
A fixed windmill has x equal to y, so p equals x times x plus four z, and primality forces x to be one.
It also rules out the boundary cases, which would need p to be a square or even.
For twenty-one, for example, there are two fixed windmills, and the argument fails, as it should.
Interesting.
But how would anyone come up with that second involution?
Honestly, from the algebra alone, I don't think I would.
But if you draw x squared plus four y z as a windmill, you see that the same outline can be cut in two different ways.
Whenever an object can be described in two ways, you get a natural pairing.
So the geometry suggests the involution, and the formula just records it.
Your proof only shows existence.
Can you actually find x and y?
Yes, the proof actually contains an algorithm.
Start at the fixed point of re-cutting and alternate the two involutions.
Each windmill has at most two neighbours, so the walk can't repeat, and it has to end at a fixed point of the swap, which is a solution.
It's like the path-following proof of Sperner's lemma.
It's slow for large primes, though, and there are faster methods using the Euclidean algorithm.
Do you know any other proof?
Yes, there's one using the Gaussian integers.
Since minus one is a square mod p, p divides n squared plus one for some n, and that factors as n plus i, times n minus i.
If p stayed prime in the Gaussian integers, it would have to divide one of those factors, which is impossible.
So p splits as a plus b i, times a minus b i, and taking norms gives p equals a squared plus b squared.
There's also Euler's proof by infinite descent, and a pigeonhole argument due to Thue.
Why is minus one a square modulo p?
By Wilson's theorem, p minus one, factorial, is minus one mod p.
Pair each number k with minus k.
When p is one mod four, the minus signs come in an even number, so the factorial of p minus one over two, squared, is minus one.
Again, it's a pairing argument.
What about sums of three squares?
That's harder, and I know the statement better than the proof.
Legendre's three-square theorem says that a positive integer is a sum of three squares unless it has the form four to the a, times eight b plus seven.
The easy half is again a congruence argument, this time mod eight.
And with four squares, Lagrange proved that every positive integer works.
Is there an application you find meaningful?
I like the connection to Pythagorean triples.
Squaring a plus b i shows that the primes that can be the hypotenuse of an integer right triangle are exactly the primes that are one mod four.
And counting lattice points in a circle even leads to Leibniz's series for pi.
Last question.
What did you learn from this theorem?
Three things.
First, you can prove existence by counting, sometimes just modulo two.
Second, sometimes you have to create a symmetry, not just find one.
And third, a good picture can turn a mysterious formula into something natural.
I first met the parity idea in Sperner's lemma, and seeing it again here made me realize it's a general strategy, not just a trick.
Let me end with what this theorem taught me.
To prove that something exists, you can count it, and sometimes counting modulo two is enough.
Symmetry is not always given.
Sometimes you have to create it.
And a good picture can turn a formula that looks like magic into something you could have discovered yourself.
Brouwer's theorem is about fixed points.
Sperner's lemma is about parity.
And Zagier's proof is about the parity of fixed points.
Ideas in mathematics keep meeting each other, and following those connections is, for me, the real joy of the subject.
Thank you for watching.
